channel.title: Medical Xpress - latest medical and health news stories
channel.description: Medical Xpress internet news portal provides the latest news on science including: Physics, Nanotechnology, Life Sciences, Space Science, Earth Science, Environment, Health and Medicine.

item.title: Alcohol, drug abuse, suicide: Is Europe really safe from America's 'deaths of despair' epidemic?
item.description: In the United States, life expectancy diverged from Europe before it stopped rising during the 2010s, even before the COVID-19 pandemic. The economists Anne Case and Angus Deaton gave a name to a phenomenon that was then booming, partly explaining this trend: "deaths of despair," which have soared since the turn of the 21st century, especially among middle-aged white people without a college degree.

item.title: Forgetful neural networks could shed light on how humans learn
item.description: How the brain learns is one of the biggest unsolved mysteries in science. Researchers in artificial intelligence from the University of Groningen (the Netherlands) and KU Leuven (Belgium) hope that a specific type of forgetting in artificial neural networks will help to capture what is happening in the human brain. The study is published in the journal Trends in Cognitive Sciences.

item.title: As measles cases mount, new report highlights safety of early vaccination for infants
item.description: As Americans prepare for holiday travel amid a nationwide measles resurgence and diminished federal public health communications, a new report from the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy's (CIDRAP's) Vaccine Integrity Project (VIP) at the University of Minnesota highlights data showing that infants as young as 6 months can safely receive the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine.

item.title: For military veterans with PTSD and alcohol use disorder, MDMA-assisted therapy may be safe, effective
item.description: The first study of a program that uses the drug MDMA to treat post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) plus alcohol use disorder in military veterans has concluded with promising results.

item.title: Regenerated bone keeps maturing after its shape is largely restored, study reveals
item.description: Regeneration is often judged by what researchers can see—whether missing tissue has returned and its shape has been restored. But a new Texas A&M study shows that bone may continue to mature mechanically beneath the surface even after it appears whole.

item.title: Your gut bacteria help your body keep track of time, and when you eat influences how much nutrition you get from food
item.description: How your body processes food is significantly influenced by daily rhythms tied to 24-hour light-dark cycles. In new research published in the journal Cell Host & Microbe, my colleagues and I found that the microbes living in your gut are the hidden timekeepers behind this system.

item.title: Alzheimer's blood marker may help estimate cognitive impairment risk up to 10 years ahead
item.description: A blood biomarker for Alzheimer's disease may help estimate a cognitively healthy person's risk of developing mild cognitive impairment or dementia over the next five or 10 years, according to a new Mayo Clinic study in JAMA Neurology.

item.title: Brain clock gene influences alcohol consumption differently in female and male mice, study shows
item.description: A gene that helps regulate the body's internal clock may influence alcohol consumption differently in males and females, according to new Concordia research.

item.title: Novel algorithm predicts brain surgery outcomes in dystonia patients
item.description: Less than 5% of patients with dystonia—a debilitating neurological movement disorder—undergo deep brain stimulation (DBS) treatment, even though it is one of the few interventions that directly target the abnormal brain processes underlying the condition. The surgical treatment is highly underutilized, likely due to its invasiveness and the lack of objective markers of who may benefit. Even among those who undergo surgery, outcomes vary widely, depending on patient characteristics and external influences.

item.title: First successful human challenge model for dengue serotype 4 could speed vaccine and drug testing
item.description: Researchers at the University of Maryland School of Medicine (UMSOM) and the Institute of Human Virology (IHV) have developed the first successful human challenge model for dengue serotype 4, a major advance that could speed the development of new drugs and vaccines against a strain of the dengue virus that remains difficult to study.

item.title: New protocol finds ways to relieve overcrowding at hospital emergency departments, study finds
item.description: According to the CDC, an average of 155 million visits to an emergency department occur in the United States every year. More than a million of those patients spend at least 24 hours at the ED. This has led to an epidemic of overcrowding.

item.title: Experimental blood test can detect four signs of deadly diseases in an hour
item.description: A new diagnostic platform is able to screen for and identify four different diseases—colorectal cancer, glioblastoma, pancreatic cancer and Alzheimer's disease—with a small amount of blood in an hour. The patent-pending technology was developed by a team of researchers led by Hsueh-Chia Chang at the University of Notre Dame.

item.title: Flu shots: Timing for maximum protection
item.description: Every year, as flu season approaches, many of us start thinking about how to protect ourselves and our loved ones from getting sick.

item.title: Newly identified kidney protein protects blood vessels, study finds
item.description: As people age, or as certain diseases progress, their blood vessels can grow stiffer and less resilient. These changes can bring an increased risk of cardiovascular disease and earlier death. One trigger for blood vessel stiffening is a higher-than-normal level of phosphate in the blood. While elevated blood phosphate (hyperphosphatemia) is not common in the general population, it is much more widespread in people with chronic kidney disease (CKD) because their kidneys lose their effectiveness at filtering out waste products.

item.title: Testing gel and a titanium brush for cleaning dental implants
item.description: Angela De Lauretis investigated how gels and a titanium brush affect protein coatings on titanium surfaces and cells' ability to adhere after cleaning. Her Ph.D. work provides knowledge that can inform the further development of methods for cleaning dental implants. The experiments were conducted in the laboratory, and the effects in patients need further investigation.

item.title: A new tool to predict T cell behavior and improve immunotherapies
item.description: T cells are the trained killers of the immune system and the driving force behind cancer immunotherapy. But the behavior of T cells is hard to predict: Some spring into action when prompted, while others become lethargic and aimless. This puzzling inconsistency is one of the main reasons immunotherapies don't work in most cancer patients.

item.title: New Public Health Alerts report spotlights how pregnant women with measles and their babies fare
item.description: With the United States teetering on the brink of losing its measles elimination status and cases across the country skyrocketing, a Public Health Alerts report today describes 112 cases of measles confirmed during pregnancy this year and last, the vast majority of them in unvaccinated women.

item.title: Why don't GLP‑1 obesity drugs work for everyone?
item.description: Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide—a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite and body weight—have become household names and important pillars in obesity management for the medical profession.

item.title: Sperm counts may be falling, but humans are unlikely to run out
item.description: For years, alarming headlines have warned that sperm counts are plummeting and humanity could be heading toward a fertility crisis. But new research suggests the picture is considerably more complicated.

item.title: Five things that shape body weight—by an obesity expert
item.description: What you eat when you're tired and hungry might come down to what's open on the way home and what you can afford. Both appetite and access to food shape decisions that can look, from the outside, like simple matters of choice.

item.title: WHO says countries need to 'move from plans to delivery' on antimicrobial resistance
item.description: New survey data released today by the World Health Organization (WHO) show that most countries have developed plans to address antimicrobial resistance (AMR). But few have implemented or provided financing for those plans.

item.title: Babies rarely see exaggerated facial expressions used in emotion research, study finds
item.description: A new paper in Communications Psychology calls into question the value of exaggerated facial expressions commonly used in research to study babies' emotional understanding. The study, led by University of Kansas researchers, shows that babies ages 6–17 months rarely encounter these expressions in everyday life—and rarely see full faces at all.

item.title: New AI approach could cut sepsis deaths and drive efficiency in emergency departments
item.description: By explaining which causes led to a patient's death, the team hopes their work will empower hospital managers to make targeted changes.

item.title: Measles is no longer considered eliminated in the US and Mexico
item.description: The U.S. has lost its measles-free status, international health officials said Tuesday, as the highly contagious virus once relegated to medical textbooks has spread—largely among the unvaccinated—at the highest rate in more than 30 years.

item.title: Review examines pain mechanisms and offers a framework for personalized treatment of endometriosis
item.description: A joint research team comprising professor Kyeong A So of the Department of Obstetrics and Gynecology at Korea University Guro Hospital and professors Jae-Wook Jeong and Tae Hoon Kim of the University of Missouri School of Medicine has comprehensively examined how pain develops and persists in patients with endometriosis. The team proposed new research directions to translate these insights into personalized treatment. Their review article was selected as a featured article in the journal Endocrine Reviews, highlighting its scientific significance and clinical relevance.

item.title: New pill combo approved for breast cancer that stops responding to hormone therapy
item.description: People with advanced breast cancer that has stopped responding to hormone therapy now have a new pill-based treatment option.

item.title: Study finds that feeling ownership of a pain-relief object may help increase pain tolerance
item.description: Pain relief may come from more than medication. A study by the Department of Psychology at Lingnan University has found that simply feeling a sense of ownership over an object believed to relieve pain may help people cope better with pain, even when the object itself contains no active ingredients. These findings have been published in The Journal of Pain and provide a new direction for exploring a low-cost approach to supporting pain management in health care.

item.title: AI may help spot early signs of lung cancer in the blood
item.description: In a blue-and-white van outside Asda last June, 68-year-old Eddie, a retired fishmonger from Fallowfield, near Manchester, received life-changing news.

item.title: Brain connectivity in high-traffic regions may shape how multiple sclerosis damages tissue
item.description: Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disorder in which the immune system mistakenly turns against the body's own cells. In this case, immune cells attack myelin, a fatty, protein-rich substance that forms a protective coating around nerve fibers. Myelin gives the brain's white matter its characteristic whitish appearance and helps nerve cells communicate with one another. However, the damage does not stop there. MS is also linked to the gradual shrinking or atrophy of gray matter, the brain tissue where most nerve cell bodies are found. As this tissue shrinks, people tend to experience more severe symptoms, including difficulties with movement and thinking.

item.title: As use of AI scribes spreads, researchers propose a framework for preparing medical trainees
item.description: Ambient AI scribes, which passively capture clinical encounters and draft notes, are among the most rapidly adopted artificial intelligence (AI) applications in health care. In one integrated health care system, they documented more than 2.5 million clinical encounters in a single year.
